clusters.canonical_name: IFEO Debugger and Port Monitor DLL Persistence
clusters.rationale: Four notes from independent atlas batches all surface the same two persistence vectors (IFEO Debugger value and Port Monitor DLL) as missing from T-017's five-layer suite.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670's Section 4 persistence curriculum covers two registry-driven autostart mechanisms absent from T-017: Image File Execution Options (IFEO) Debugger value and Port Monitor DLLs. IFEO persistence writes HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<target.exe>\Debugger to redirect process launch into an attacker binary (Lab 4.3 'IFEOPersist'). Port Monitor persistence installs a DLL via the AddMonitor() API into HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors\<name>\Driver, which the Print Spooler service loads at spooler initialization. Both are file-less, event-driven persistence vectors triggered by legitimate system events (process launch, spooler restart) rather than scheduled timers. Multiple SEC670 modules independently converge on these as standalone techniques distinct from Run keys or COM hijack.
clusters.technical_anchor: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<binary>\Debugger + AddMonitor() → HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control rint\Monitors
clusters.priority_reason: 4 member notes from independent batches, named techniques with public tooling and lab exercises

clusters.rationale: Two notes converge on SilentProcessExit monitoring as a persistence trigger distinct from IFEO Debugger, both citing it as a coverage gap in T-017.
clusters.consolidated_description: SilentProcessExit is a registry-driven persistence mechanism triggered when a monitored process terminates, using the GlobalFlag value in HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options\<binary>\GlobalFlag to enable silent process exit monitoring, and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit\<binary>\ReportingMode and MonitorProcess values to specify the action on exit. SEC670's Lab 4.3 covers this as a paired variant of IFEO Debugger persistence — the Debugger value triggers on launch, SilentProcessExit triggers on termination. T-017's five-layer suite (COM hijack, NTFS EA, schtask, TLS callback, PhantomPersist) does not document this mechanism. The GFlags-based enablement is shared with the IFEO Debugger variant, making the two operationally complementary for launch-and-exit coverage.
clusters.technical_anchor: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SilentProcessExit\<binary>\ReportingMode + GlobalFlag FLG_MONITOR_SILENT_PROCESS_EXIT
clusters.priority_reason: 2 member notes, named technique with dedicated lab exercise, fills a distinct event-driven gap

clusters.rationale: Singleton surfacing WMI event subscription as an event-driven fileless persistence layer missing from T-017, distinct from IFEO and Port Monitor in trigger mechanism.
clusters.consolidated_description: WMI permanent event subscriptions provide fileless persistence through __EventFilter → __EventConsumer binding via __FilterToConsumerBinding, with CommandLineEventConsumer executing an attacker payload when the filter condition fires. The filter can be any WQL query against system state (e.g., SELECT * FROM __InstanceModificationEvent WITHIN 60 WHERE TargetInstance ISA 'Win32_PerfFormattedData_PerfOS_System' for timer-based triggers). This mechanism loads no DLL, writes no Run key, and runs inside the WMI provider host (wmiprvse.exe), making it architecturally distinct from the registry-driven layers in T-017. SEC670 identifies this alongside port monitor and IFEO as event-driven persistence vectors that T-017's scheduled and registry-based layers do not cover.
clusters.technical_anchor: __EventFilter + CommandLineEventConsumer + __FilterToConsumerBinding in root\subscription namespace
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton with named MITRE ATT&CK technique (T1546.003), high operational stealth, fills event-driven gap

clusters.rationale: Four notes from independent batches all identify CreateService + SCM as a persistence vector absent from T-017's documented five layers.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 Book 4 documents the full SCM persistence lifecycle: OpenSCManager() → CreateService(hSCManager, lpServiceName, NULL, SERVICE_ALL_ACCESS, SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS, SERVICE_AUTO_START, SERVICE_ERROR_NORMAL, lpBinaryPathName, ...) with Lab 4.1 'PersistentService' walking through a custom service binary. The service auto-restarts on boot via SERVICE_AUTO_START, and failure-action recovery can be configured via ChangeServiceConfig to restart on crash. This is the most commonly deployed persistence vector in real-world intrusions (SEC670 review material identifies Run key and services as the two most common), yet T-017 documents COM hijack, NTFS EA, schtask, TLS callback, and PhantomPersist without including the SCM layer.
clusters.technical_anchor: CreateService(hSCManager, lpServiceName, dwServiceType=SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS, dwStartType=SERVICE_AUTO_START, lpBinaryPathName)
clusters.priority_reason: 4 member notes from independent batches, most commonly deployed persistence vector in real intrusions

clusters.rationale: Three notes converge on Run/RunOnce registry keys as the most commonly used persistence key, absent from T-017's documented layers.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 review material explicitly identifies HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run as the most commonly used registry persistence key, with HKLM requiring administrator privileges. The RunOnce variant (...\RunOnce) executes its entries once and then deletes the value, providing single-shot persistence. T-017's five-layer persistence suite does not include Run/RunOnce despite their prevalence in real-world intrusions (SEC670 cites APT28, Emotet, APT39 as users of registry-based persistence). The HKCU\...\Run variant provides per-user persistence without elevation, making it accessible from medium-IL implant contexts. SEC670 devotes an entire module to registry-based persistence covering Run, RunOnce, RunOnceEx, and the distinction between HKLM (admin) and HKCU (user) scopes.
clusters.technical_anchor: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run + HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce (single-shot, auto-deleted)
clusters.priority_reason: 3 member notes, most commonly used registry persistence key, cited APT usage

clusters.canonical_name: AppInit_DLLs and AppCert DLL Registry Loading
clusters.rationale: Two notes converge on AppInit_DLLs and AppCert DLLs as registry-driven DLL loading mechanisms distinct from Run keys, both absent from T-017.
clusters.consolidated_description: AppInit_DLLs (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs and RequireSignedAppInit_DLLs) causes user32.dll to load the specified DLL into any process that imports user32.dll, providing broad-scope persistence across GUI processes. AppCert DLLs (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCertDlls) similarly loads DLLs into processes that use the Win32 subsystem APIs via CreateProcess. SEC670 treats these as distinct from Run/RunOnce keys because they are DLL-loading mechanisms triggered by subsystem events rather than shell-launch values. AppInit_DLLs in particular is historically significant (Apt28/T9000 usage documented by SEC670) but has been progressively restricted by Microsoft (RequireSignedAppInit DLLs, Secure Boot mitigation disabling AppInit entirely on modern systems).
clusters.technical_anchor: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs (loaded by user32.dll DllMain) + HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\AppCertDlls
clusters.priority_reason: 2 member notes, distinct DLL-loading mechanism with historical APT usage, increasingly mitigated on modern systems

clusters.canonical_name: Service Hiding via SDDL/DACL Security Descriptor Tampering
clusters.rationale: Two notes converge on modifying service object DACLs to hide persistence from enumeration while retaining start capability.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 documents SDDL (Security Descriptor Definition Language) string syntax for service objects: ace_type;ace_flags;rights;object_guid;inherit_object_guid;account_sid, where the rights token controls access (e.g., RC=Read Config, DC=Delete/Config, CC=Create Child). Using sc.exe sdset <service> D:(A;;DC;;;AU) or SetNamedSecurityInfo with DACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION, an operator can deny SERVICE_QUERY_STATUS and SERVICE_ENUMERATE_DEPENDENTS to 'Everyone' or 'INTERACTIVE', causing the service to be invisible to sc query, services.msc, and Get-Service enumeration. The service remains startable by an operator who retains SERVICE_START in their own ACE. This is a persistence resilience measure layered on top of service-based persistence (CreateService), not a standalone autostart mechanism. The vault's T-016 and T-017 do not document this stealth hardening.
clusters.technical_anchor: sc.exe sdset / SetNamedSecurityInfo(DACL_SECURITY_INFORMATION) with SDDL string denying SERVICE_QUERY_STATUS to 'INTERACTIVE' sid
clusters.priority_reason: 2 member notes, distinct stealth hardening technique with concrete API surface

clusters.canonical_name: Service Architecture, Unquoted Path, and SCM Suspended-Start Internals
clusters.rationale: Three notes all touch service internals — shared/own/isolated archetype, unquoted binary path exploitation, and SCM suspended-start housekeeping sequence — as prerequisites for both persistence and injection target selection.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 surfaces three service-internal concepts that the vault does not document: (1) SERVICE_WIN32_SHARE_PROCESS vs SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS vs SERVICE_WIN32_OWN_PROCESS (isolated) archetypes from QueryServiceConfig2 dwServiceType affect injection target selection — an injected shared svchost crashes all cohabiting services, while an isolated own-process service contains the blast radius. (2) Unquoted service binary paths (lpBinaryPathName containing spaces without quotes, e.g., C:\Program Files\My Service\srv.exe) enable privilege escalation via path traversal when Windows resolves the binary. (3) SCM performs a five-step housekeeping sequence on service start including creating the service process in a suspended state (CREATE_SUSPENDED) and resuming after mapping the binary, described as 'process-hollowing-like' semantics that create a hook-free window. All three are documented in SEC670 review and lab material as prerequisite knowledge for service-based operations.
clusters.technical_anchor: QueryServiceConfig2(dwServiceType) SERVICE_WIN32_SHARE_PROCESS vs OWN_PROCESS + unquoted lpBinaryPathName + SCM CREATE_SUSPENDED during StartService housekeeping
clusters.priority_reason: 3 member notes covering distinct service internals topics that serve as prerequisites for multiple techniques

clusters.rationale: Singleton documenting the ITaskScheduler COM interface as a schtasks.exe-free enumeration path, distinct from T-017's task creation focus.
clusters.consolidated_description: The ITaskScheduler COM interface provides programmatic access to Task Scheduler v1.0 tasks without spawning schtasks.exe: ITaskScheduler::NewWorkItem creates tasks, ITaskScheduler::Enum returns an IEnumWorkItems enumerator whose Next() method yields task names. This COM path avoids the schtasks.exe telemetry surface (process creation, command-line logging via EID 4688) that the vault's T-017 schtask persistence layer would trigger if it uses the CLI. The vault documents schtask persistence via the task creation path but does not cover the enumeration counterpart via COM, which is relevant for both discovery (T-023) and persistence-resilience verification (T-017). The ITaskScheduler interface is available on all Windows versions and resolves to taskschd.dll via CoCreateInstance with CLSID {148BD52A-A2AB-11CE-B11F-00AA00530503}.
clusters.technical_anchor: ITaskScheduler::Enum → IEnumWorkItems::Next() with CLSID {148BD52A-A2AB-11CE-B11F-00AA00530503}
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton, niche enumeration path, but provides concrete COM-based alternative to telemetry-heavy CLI

clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note documenting RegNotifyChangeKeyValue as an event-driven execution trigger mechanism.
clusters.consolidated_description: RegNotifyChangeKeyValue(hKey, bWatchSubtree, dwNotifyFilter, hEvent, REG_NOTIFY_THREAD_AGNOSTIC) registers a wait event that fires when the monitored registry key or value changes, providing an event-driven trigger that does not require polling. SEC670 frames this defensively (detecting registry modifications) but the same primitive enables an attacker-side execution trigger: a watchdog thread waiting on hEvent can execute a payload when a specific registry value is modified by any process, including legitimate system maintenance. The REG_NOTIFY_THREAD_AGNOSTIC flag (Windows 8+) allows the notification to persist across thread termination. This is architecturally distinct from Run keys (value-on-launch) and WMI subscriptions (WQL filter) — it triggers on external write events to an attacker-chosen key, providing a fileless, low-frequency execution channel.
clusters.technical_anchor: RegNotifyChangeKeyValue(hKey, REG_NOTIFY_THREAD_AGNOSTIC, REG_NOTIFY_CHANGE_LAST_SET, hEvent)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but emerging tradecraft with concrete API and distinct trigger mechanism from existing persistence layers

clusters.canonical_name: Disk Artifact Placement and Blending Tradecraft
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note documenting SEC670's disk placement curriculum, distinct from runtime anti-analysis.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 dedicates material to where on disk to place dropped binaries and blending rules for file-based OPSEC. Placement options include Desktop, Documents, Downloads, AppData, Program Files, and System32, each with different detection-surface tradeoffs. Blending rules include 'do not be the first or last file created' and 'timestamp within the existing file population distribution' to evade timeline analysis. The vault's T-021 (Artifact Suite) and T-020 (Anti-Analysis) do not currently document the disk-placement tradecraft curriculum. This is a distinct anti-analysis category from runtime techniques (anti-debug, anti-VM) — it concerns post-disk-persistence forensic blending. Relevant API surface includes SetFileTime for timestamp manipulation and NtSetInformationFile for FileBasicInformation attribute modification.
clusters.technical_anchor: SetFileTime(lpFileTime, NULL, NULL, lpLastWriteTime) + NtSetInformationFile(FileBasicInformation) for timestamp blending
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton, OPSEC tradecraft rather than technique, but fills a documented curriculum gap

clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note documenting a novel category — protecting implants from reverse engineering if captured on disk, distinct from runtime anti-analysis.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 references the PoC tool 'Skrull' as an example of 'DRMing' an implant — applying encryption, anti-tamper, and integrity checks to the implant binary itself so that if it is captured on disk by a defender or sandbox, it cannot be reverse-engineered or have its C2 configuration extracted. This represents an emerging tradecraft category distinct from runtime anti-analysis (anti-debug, anti-VM): it is a static-protection measure applied to the artifact at build time. The mechanism typically involves encrypting the .text section or embedding the C2 configuration as an encrypted blob keyed to a runtime-decodable secret (e.g., hardware ID, domain-joined machine SID). The vault's T-020 anti-analysis suite does not document this capture-resistance layer, which is increasingly relevant as defenders improve at extracting C2 configs from captured binaries.
clusters.technical_anchor: Encrypted .text section / C2 config blob keyed to machine-specific secret (e.g., SID via GetComputerName + CryptDeriveKey)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but novel emerging tradecraft category not in existing T-001..T-074, with named public PoC

clusters.rationale: Singleton cross-source-convergence note documenting the canonical four-step injection pattern as a pedagogical baseline across SEC670 and MalDev Academy.
clusters.consolidated_description: The classic four-step CreateRemoteThread DLL injection flow — OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) → VirtualAllocEx(PAGE_READWRITE) → WriteProcessMemory(dllPath) → CreateRemoteThread(LoadLibrary, dllPath) — appears as the introductory walk-through across multiple SEC670 units and is the foundational pattern that MalDev Academy builds upon for more advanced techniques. While heavily detected by modern EDR (OpenProcess kernel callback, VirtualAllocEx ETW, CreateRemoteThread kernel callback), this pattern is the pedagogical baseline that contextualizes the vault's T-013 injection methods. The convergence across SEC670 and MalDev Academy confirms this as the canonical teaching sequence from which more advanced techniques (early bird APC, thread hijacking, module stomping) diverge.
clusters.technical_anchor: CreateRemoteThread(hProcess, 0, 0, LoadLibraryA, lpDllPathBuffer, 0, NULL)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton, heavily detected baseline technique, but provides pedagogical context for T-013's advanced methods

clusters.canonical_name: PE Injection (Additional Image Loading) vs Process Hollowing
clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note documenting the distinction between loading an additional PE image and replacing the target image.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 explicitly distinguishes PE Injection — loading an additional PE image into a running process's address space — from process hollowing, which replaces the target process's primary image. PE injection maps a new section (NtMapViewOfSection or VirtualAllocEx + manual PE loader) into the host process without destroying the original image, allowing the injected PE to coexist with the host's legitimate code. Process hollowing (CreateProcess suspended → unmap original → map replacement → resume) replaces the image entirely, leaving no trace of the original binary. T-013 groups process hollowing with other methods but does not call out PE injection as a distinct technique. The distinction matters for detection: PE injection leaves the host's PEB->ImageBase pointing at the original image while the injected PE is a secondary mapping, whereas hollowing updates (or should update) the PEB to point at the replacement.
clusters.technical_anchor: NtMapViewOfSection(SectionHandle, ProcessHandle, BaseAddress, ...) for additional image vs NtUnmapViewOfSection for hollowing replacement
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a distinct injection variant with different PEB/detection surface from hollowing

clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note documenting session-ID-based target selection for cross-session injection, distinct from same-session methods.
clusters.consolidated_description: WTSEnumerateProcessesEx(WTS_CURRENT_SERVER_HANDLE, WTS_PROCESS_INFO_LEVEL_1, &ppProcessInfo, &pCount) returns a WTS_PROCESS_INFOW per process that includes the session identifier, allowing an operator to select an injection target in a different logon session (e.g., Session 1 from a Session 0 beacon, or a different user's session). Cross-session injection requires SeDebugPrivilege to OpenProcess across session boundaries, and the resulting thread runs in the target session's window station and desktop. The vault's injection cards (T-007, T-012, T-013) do not document session boundary as a target selection criterion, though T-023 (Process Recon) enumerates sessions. This technique is operationally significant for lateral movement within a single host (e.g., injecting into a user's explorer.exe from a SYSTEM context beacon to operate in the interactive desktop).
clusters.technical_anchor: WTSEnumerateProcessesEx → WTS_PROCESS_INFOW.SessionId + OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) across session boundary with SeDebugPrivilege
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a distinct targeting dimension not covered in existing injection cards

clusters.rationale: Cross-source convergence between SEC670 and CRTO on abusing leaked high-privilege handles to bypass OpenProcess telemetry.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 and CRTO both surface the abuse of leaked high-privilege handles (e.g., a third-party process holding a SYSTEM PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS handle to a high-value target) as a way to inject shellcode without calling OpenProcess, bypassing the PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine / ObRegisterCallbacks detection surface for process handle acquisition. The operator locates the leaked handle via NtQuerySystemInformation(SystemHandleInformation) which returns a SYSTEM_HANDLE_TABLE_ENTRY_INFO array including process PIDs, handle values, and granted access masks. DuplicateHandle(sourceProcessHandle, sourceHandle, currentProcess, &targetHandle, 0, FALSE, DUPLICATE_SAME_ACCESS) transfers the handle into the operator's process, after which VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread or NtQueueApcThread can proceed without any OpenProcess call. This is a high-value technique because the ObRegisterCallbacks callback (the primary EDR mechanism for process handle monitoring) does not fire for DuplicateHandle transfers of existing handles.
clusters.technical_anchor: NtQuerySystemInformation(SystemHandleInformation) → SYSTEM_HANDLE_TABLE_ENTRY_INFO → DuplicateHandle(DUPLICATE_SAME_ACCESS)
clusters.priority_reason: Cross-source convergence, bypasses ObRegisterCallbacks handle monitoring, novel primitive not in T-001..T-074

clusters.rationale: Four notes from independent batches converge on Volatility, PE-sieve, and Moneta as the named defensive tool suite that the vault does not reference.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 explicitly names Volatility, PE-sieve, and Moneta as the memory forensics suite defenders use to identify in-memory and fileless execution artifacts. PE-sieve (hasherezade) scans a process's memory for PE images, compares in-memory headers against on-disk counterparts, and flags unmapped/scraped/hollowed images by comparing the .text section bytes in memory against the file on disk. Volatility performs full-memory analysis of EPROCESS blocks, VAD (Virtual Address Descriptor) trees, and PEB structures to identify injected code, hollowed processes, and unbacked executable regions. Moneta scans for unbacked executable memory (VirtualAlloc'd without a file backing) and suspicious RWX regions. SEC670 explicitly identifies memory forensics as the defensive counter to in-memory execution (citing WannaCry and EternalBlue). The vault's T-016, T-013, and T-007 document EDR evasion from the product perspective (ETW-TI, kernel callbacks, hooks) but do not reference these standalone forensic tools. This gap matters because an operator who defeats the EDR's runtime monitoring can still be caught by a post-capture memory forensic scan.
clusters.technical_anchor: PE-sieve: in-memory vs on-disk .text section byte comparison via NtReadVirtualMemory; Volatility: EPROCESS VAD tree + PEB ImageBaseAddress walk
clusters.priority_reason: 4 member notes from independent batches, named defensive tools that define the post-capture detection surface

clusters.canonical_name: Process Enumeration API Tradeoffs (EnumProcesses / Toolhelp / WTS / NtQuerySystemInformation)
clusters.rationale: Singleton documenting the systematic comparison of four enumeration APIs and their detection-surface tradeoffs.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 systematically compares EnumProcesses (K32EnumProcesses, simple PID array, no parent/PPID), CreateToolhelp32Snapshot (TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS, full PROCESSENTRY32 with parent PID, requires snapshot), WTSEnumerateProcesses (WTS API, includes session ID, server-scoped), and NtQuerySystemInformation(SystemProcessInformation, class 5, returns SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION with thread list, handle count, IO counters). The snapshot variant (Toolhelp) is identified as the most complete for process-tree reconstruction (parent/child), while NtQuerySystemInformation returns the richest per-process data (thread enumeration, kernel time, IO counters) without a snapshot handle. Each API has different EDR telemetry: EnumProcesses and WTSEnumerateProcesses are well-known and lightly monitored, while NtQuerySystemInformation with class 5 is a direct syscall (bypassing userland hooks) but may be flagged by ETW-TI if the information class is considered sensitive. The vault's T-023 and T-020 do not document this API selection tradeoff.
clusters.technical_anchor: NtQuerySystemInformation(SystemProcessInformation=class 5) → SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION with NextEntryOffset chain + CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents API selection tradeoffs with direct detection-surface implications

clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note documenting KUSER_SHARED_DATA at VA 0x7FFE0000 as a syscall-free recon primitive, analogous to T-004's PEB walker.
clusters.consolidated_description: KUSER_SHARED_DATA is a fixed user-mode mapping at virtual address 0x7FFE0000 (linear-mapped read-only page shared between user mode and kernel) that exposes system metadata without any syscall. The KUSER_SHARED_DATA structure (defined in ntddk.h) includes fields like NtMajorVersion, NtMinorVersion, SystemRoot (UnicodeString pointing to L'\SystemRoot'), ProductType, SoftwareBuiltOnBootId, and most critically, TickCount and SystemTime for high-frequency timing queries without the overhead of NtQuerySystemTime or GetTickCount. SEC670's review question placing KUSER_SHARED_DATA at 0x7FFE0000 documents this as a fixed-address primitive analogous to the TEB/PEB walker (T-004) — both are syscall-free data access paths into kernel-maintained structures. The vault's T-004 PEB Walker relies on the analogous fixed TEB→PEB pointer chain (GS:[0x30]→TEB→PEB), and KUSER_SHARED_DATA is the second fixed user-mode mapping that bypasses syscall-level telemetry entirely.
clusters.technical_anchor: KUSER_SHARED_DATA at VA 0x7FFE0000 — fields: SystemTime (offset 0x14), TickCount (offset 0x10), SystemRoot (UnicodeString at offset varies by build)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents a fixed-address recon primitive that bypasses all syscall telemetry, complements T-004 PEB walker

clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note documenting HKPD as a registry root key inaccessible via regedit, requiring RegQueryValueEx.
clusters.consolidated_description: HKEY_PERFORMANCE_DATA (HKPD, handle value 0x80000004 on pre-Win10, or the PERFLIB namespace on modern builds) is the only registry root key that cannot be accessed via regedit.exe — it must be queried via RegQueryValueEx(HKEY_PERFORMANCE_DATA, lpValueName, ...) and the returned data is supplied dynamically by perfmon providers (DLLs registered in HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Perflib\<lang>\Counter) rather than stored in the registry hive. This makes HKPD a programmatic-only access path with a different detection surface from standard registry access: RegQueryValueEx on HKPD triggers Perflib DLL loading, which can be used for both recon (system performance counters expose process/thread/IO statistics) and as an alternative registry access surface that bypasses registry-monitoring EDR hooks targeting standard hive access (HKLM, HKCU). The vault's T-023 and T-020 do not document this access quirk.
clusters.technical_anchor: RegQueryValueEx(HKEY_PERFORMANCE_DATA=0x80000004, lpValueName, lpcbData) — data supplied by Perflib provider DLLs, not registry hive storage
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton, niche access quirk, but provides alternative registry recon surface with distinct detection profile

clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note identifying foundational Windows internals vocabulary (WIN32_FIND_DATA, KUSER_SHARED_DATA, etc.) as reference material that would make T-NNN cards navigable.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 units 13–21 and 24–25 are review-question material that surfaces foundational Windows internals vocabulary the vault does not have reference cards for: WIN32_FIND_DATA (FindFirstFile/FindNextFile output structure), KUSER_SHARED_DATA (fixed user-mode mapping at 0x7FFE0000), PROCESSENTRY32 (CreateToolhelp32Snapshot output), SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY (StartServiceCtrlDispatcher input), and SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION (NtQuerySystemInformation class 5 output). These are not techniques but concept/reference nodes — documenting their field layouts, sizes, and version differences would make several T-NNN cards navigable for readers without prior Windows internals background. For example, T-023 process recon uses these structures directly, and T-017 persistence references SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY for service binary integration.
clusters.technical_anchor: WIN32_FIND_DATA (FindFirstFileW output), SYSTEM_PROCESS_INFORMATION (NtQuerySystemInformation class 5), SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY (StartServiceCtrlDispatcher)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton, concept/reference material with educational rather than operational value, tier C

clusters.canonical_name: APC Queue and Thread State Internals
clusters.rationale: Singleton cross-source-convergence note documenting APC queue mechanics and thread Ready/Running/Waiting states as internals prerequisite for injection techniques.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 review material identifies the APC (Asynchronous Procedure Call) queue as the mechanism that lets threads process routines during their quantum, and thread Ready/Running/Waiting states as the scheduling context that determines when an APC is delivered. The KTHREAD structure (kernel) contains two APC queues: the UserApcPending flag and the ApcState.UserApcListHead — when a thread enters an alertable wait (WaitForSingleObjectEx with bAlertable=TRUE, or SleepEx with alertable), the kernel drains the user-mode APC queue, calling each APC routine in the thread's user-mode context. Thread states (Ready, Running, Waiting) are tracked in KTHREAD.State (values 0–7: Initialized, Ready, Running, Standby, Terminated, Waiting, Transition, DeferredReady) and determine APC deliverability. This is prerequisite internals knowledge for the vault's T-007 Early Bird APC and T-012 thread hijacking techniques — both rely on queuing an APC (NtQueueApcThread) that is delivered when the target enters an alertable state or during thread initialization.
clusters.technical_anchor: KTHREAD.ApcState.UserApcListHead + UserApcPending flag; thread alertable wait via WaitForSingleObjectEx(bAlertable=TRUE) or KeWaitForSingleObject(UserRequest)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents internals prerequisite for multiple injection techniques (Early Bird, thread hijack, APC)

clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note documenting a general primitive: a Medium-IL process can auto-enable held privileges without UAC elevation.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670's SeTimeZonePrivilege example demonstrates a Medium-IL process auto-enabling a held privilege without UAC elevation: LookupPrivilegeValue obtains the LUID, AdjustTokenPrivileges(TokenHandle, FALSE, &tp, ...) sets the privilege to SE_PRIVILEGE_ENABLED, and the privilege is active without any UAC consent prompt. This illustrates a general primitive: a token may hold a privilege in Disabled state (LUID present in TOKEN_PRIVILEGES but not enabled), and a Medium-IL process can enable it via AdjustTokenPrivileges if the privilege is already present in the token. Privileges like SeTimeZonePrivilege, SeChangeNotifyPrivilege, SeShutdownPrivilege are commonly held but disabled in medium-integrity tokens and can be enabled without elevation. This is distinct from UAC bypass (T-015) — no elevation occurs, the privilege was already present; the operator simply activates it. The vault does not document this privilege-enablement primitive.
clusters.technical_anchor: AdjustTokenPrivileges(TokenHandle, FALSE, &TOKEN_PRIVILEGES{PrivilegeCount=1, Privileges[0].Luid, SE_PRIVILEGE_ENABLED}, ...)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but novel primitive not in T-001..T-074, documented with specific privilege example

clusters.canonical_name: Suspended Process Creation as Hook-Free Window
clusters.rationale: Singleton emerging-tradecraft note documenting the suspended stage of process creation as the moment free from EDR hooks, explaining why hollowing/early-bird/hijacking work.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 review questions explicitly identify the suspended stage of process creation (between NtCreateProcessEx returning the handle with CREATE_SUSPENDED and the first instruction executing) as the moment free from EDR userland hooks. During this window, the process PEB is initialized, the loader (ntdll!LdrInitializeThunk) has not yet run, and no EDR DLL has been injected via standard AppInit/AppCert/known-dlls mechanisms. This is the operational reason why process hollowing (CreateProcess suspended → NtUnmapViewOfSection → NtMapViewOfSection replacement → ResumeThread), Early Bird APC (NtQueueApcThread before ResumeThread — the APC fires in ntdll!LdrInitializeThunk before EDR hooks are installed), and thread hijacking (SuspendThread → GetThreadContext → SetThreadContext → ResumeThread) all work: they operate in the pre-hook window. The vault's T-012, T-013, and T-016 do not explicitly document this temporal window as the evasion mechanism.
clusters.technical_anchor: CREATE_SUSPENDED flag in NtCreateProcessEx → suspended window before ntdll!LdrInitializeThunk installs EDR hooks
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the temporal evasion mechanism underlying multiple existing injection techniques

clusters.canonical_name: Kernel Residual Monitoring After Userland Unhooking
clusters.rationale: Singleton cross-source-convergence note addressing the question of whether unhooking truly blinds an EDR, converging with broader evasion literature.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 explicitly addresses the question of whether unhooking ntdll truly blinds a security product, with the answer being that a kernel module may still be watching. After restoring ntdll.dll from a clean copy (mapping \KnownDlls\ntdll.dll or reading from disk and restoring the .text section), userland hooks in ntdll are cleared, but the EDR's kernel-mode components remain: ObRegisterCallbacks (process/thread handle creation monitoring), PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine (process creation/exit), PsSetCreateThreadNotifyRoutine (thread creation), PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine (module loading), and ETW-TI (Trace Intelligence — NtTraceEvent kernel callbacks). Additionally, the EDR may register a file-system minifilter (FltRegisterFilter) that monitors disk I/O, and a registry callback (CmRegisterCallbackEx) for registry writes. The vault's T-016 documents userland unhooking but does not document this residual kernel monitoring surface as the reason unhooking alone is insufficient.
clusters.technical_anchor: ObRegisterCallbacks + PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine + PsSetCreateThreadNotifyRoutine + PsSetLoadImageNotifyRoutine + ETW-TI (NtTraceEvent)
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but documents the critical residual detection surface that limits the value of userland unhooking

clusters.canonical_name: Custom Loader Development and Unhook→Bypass→C2 Callback Arc
clusters.rationale: Two notes converge on SEC670 Section 5's custom loader curriculum sequencing loader development, unhooking, AMSI patching, and C2 callback establishment as a single operational arc.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 Section 5 (units 27–29, 32–37) sequences custom loader development, ntdll unhooking, AV/EDR bypass, AMSI patching, and C2 callback establishment as a single training arc. The loader is the initial execution vehicle — a custom PE that manually maps and executes the implant payload (manual PE loader: NtCreateFile → NtReadFile → parse PE headers → NtAllocateVirtualMemory → copy sections → resolve imports via NtAllocateVirtualMemory + LdrLoadDll → fix relocations → DllMain(ATTACH)). This sequencing mirrors the operational reality: the loader must establish execution (manual mapping), defeat runtime monitoring (unhook ntdll, patch amsi.dll!AmsiScanBuffer), and then establish C2 callback registration before the implant can phone home. The vault's dark_crystal crate contains loader infrastructure but T-016 does not document the full arc from loader development through C2 callback as an integrated discipline.
clusters.technical_anchor: Manual PE loader: NtAllocateVirtualMemory → section copy → IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_IMPORT LdrLoadDll resolution → DllMain(ATTACH) + ntdll unhook + amsi.dll!AmsiScanBuffer patch
clusters.priority_reason: 2 member notes documenting an integrated operational arc that spans loader, evasion, and C2

clusters.canonical_name: Capability Staging OPSEC — Reflective vs Disk
clusters.rationale: Two notes converge across SEC670, MalDev Academy, and CRTO on the principle that capabilities should not be dropped to disk on systems with unknown security posture.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 frames dropping a capability to disk as risking both detection (file-system minifilter, Windows Defender real-time protection) and loss of capability (the staged binary is a recoverable artifact for defenders). The convergence across SEC670, MalDev Academy, and CRTO is that capabilities should prefer reflective loading (RtlImageNtHeader + manual PE mapping in-process) over disk staging on systems with unknown security products. The vault documents file-less execution techniques (T-013 in-memory, T-016 evasion) and artifact management (T-009, T-010) but does not frame the staging decision as an explicit OPSEC tradeoff with dual failure modes. SEC670's framing — detection AND capability loss as equivalent failures — changes the operator's risk calculus: a staged capability that is detected is not merely burned, it is actively counterproductive because it provides the defender with a recoverable sample.
clusters.technical_anchor: Reflective loading via RtlImageNtHeader(NT headers) → NtAllocateVirtualMemory(PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE) → section copy → import resolution — vs disk staging via NtCreateFile + NtWriteFile
clusters.priority_reason: 2 member notes with cross-source convergence across SEC670/MalDev/CRTO, documents an OPSEC decision framework

clusters.canonical_name: Malleable C2 Profile and P2P Listener Convergence
clusters.rationale: Two notes converge on CRTO's C2 tradecraft — malleable profiles for HTTP traffic shaping and P2P listener chaining for lateral beaconing.
clusters.consolidated_description: CRTO describes malleable C2 profiles as the canonical HTTP-beacon traffic-shaping mechanism (Cobalt Strike's .profile files controlling User-Agent, URI, headers, jitter, GET/POST staging) and the vault's T-022 implements a malleable C2 profile engine (henge.rs). CRTO also documents P2P listeners chaining Beacons over TCP (tcp listener) and SMB named pipes (smb listener), plus a C2 Matrix spanning HTTP(S), DNS, TCP, and SMB transports. The convergence between CRTO's operational framing and the vault's T-022 implementation confirms malleable profiles and P2P chaining as the standard C2 architecture. The P2P chaining is operationally significant because it allows a beacon that cannot egress directly (e.g., isolated subnet) to chain through an intermediate beacon that has HTTP egress, using the SMB or TCP listener as the transport.
clusters.technical_anchor: Cobalt Strike .profile (HTTP traffic shaping: User-Agent, URI, jitter) + P2P: tcp listener (bind TCP) + smb listener (\.\pipe\msagent_* named pipe)
clusters.priority_reason: 2 member notes with cross-source convergence, confirms T-022 architecture against CRTO operational framing

clusters.canonical_name: Named Pipes as C2 Transport Substrate
clusters.rationale: Singleton cross-source-convergence note documenting named pipes as a duplex, network-capable C2 transport absent from T-022's transport list.
clusters.consolidated_description: Multiple SEC670 slides cover named pipes as duplex, network-capable IPC primitives dependent on the Server service (lanmanserver). Named pipes for C2 use CreateNamedPipe(\\.\pipe\<name>, PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX, PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE | PIPE_WAIT, ...) on the listener side and CreateFile(\\<target>\pipe\<name>, GENERIC_READ | GENERIC_WRITE, ...) on the client side, with network access via the IPC$ share. The vault's T-022 networking suite lists NT sockets but does not explicitly surface named pipes as a C2 transport. Named pipes are operationally distinct from TCP sockets: they use the SMB protocol (port 445), authenticate via the target's token (not the beacon's), and can traverse NAT/network boundaries where the Server service is exposed. Cobalt Strike's smb beacon and CRTO's P2P chaining (convergent note above) both use named pipes as the transport.
clusters.technical_anchor: CreateNamedPipe(\\.\pipe\<name>, PIPE_ACCESS_DUPLEX, PIPE_TYPE_MESSAGE) + CreateFile(\\<target>\pipe\<name>) via SMB IPC$
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton but cross-source convergence, named pipe C2 is a canonical transport used by Cobalt Strike and CRTO

clusters.rationale: Singleton coverage-gap note documenting the operational principle that an implant must initiate C2 contact, framing T-019 and T-022.
clusters.consolidated_description: SEC670 frames 'Calling Home' as the foundational operational principle that an implant must initiate contact with its C2 infrastructure — without this step, the implant is 'lost and forgotten.' This is the operational prerequisite for the vault's T-022 networking transports (HTTP, DNS, TCP, named pipe) and T-019 (beacon loop / sleep cycle). The calling-home step encompasses beacon registration (sending system info, implant ID, build ID), tasking retrieval (pull or push model), and heartbeat establishment (jittered sleep interval). The vault documents the C2 transports (T-022) and the beacon loop (T-019) but does not document the calling-home bootstrap as the operational bridge between initial execution (T-016 loader arc) and steady-state C2 (T-019). This is the step where the implant transitions from a deployed payload to a networked asset under operator control.
clusters.technical_anchor: Beacon registration: HTTP POST /register with system_info (hostname, IP, user, OS build) + implant_id → C2 returns tasking or sleep interval
clusters.priority_reason: Singleton, operational principle rather than technique, but bridges T-016 execution and T-019/T-022 C2
